The first time I noticed time doing something strange, it wasn’t dramatic. There were no clocks exploding, no sudden lightning strikes, no cinematic twist where the world flips and we realize we’re living inside a loop. It was subtler than that—like discovering a small draft under a door and only later realizing you’ve been letting the wrong kind of cold in all winter.

I was standing in a grocery store aisle, holding a basket I didn’t really need, reading labels the way people read fortunes. Tomato sauce, cans of beans, cereal boxes with cartoon characters smiling too widely. Nothing in particular required my attention, and yet I kept pausing as if my body had found a rhythm my mind couldn’t name. The overhead lights hummed. Somewhere near the front, a child cried and then stopped quickly, as if someone had gently pressed a hand over their voice. The air smelled like oranges and floor cleaner.

Then I looked at the wall clock.

It was just a regular analog clock, white face, black hands, the kind you see in places that have decided punctuality isn’t a priority but existence is. The second hand moved, as it should. But between one tick and the next—between two small movements of metal—something happened that didn’t fit the ordinary physics of seconds.

Not that the seconds didn’t pass. They did. It’s just that the moment felt… thick. Like honey. Like the world had paused just long enough for me to notice my own attention moving through it. I blinked, and the clock continued. The cashier was already calling someone’s name. Someone’s cart squeaked. The crying resumed briefly, then ceased again.

I remember thinking: *So that’s what you miss when you don’t pay attention.*

After that, I started noticing time everywhere. Not as a haunting or a prophecy, but as an everyday substance. When I walked too fast, time felt sharp—cutting. When I moved slowly, it felt softer. In conversation, time expanded when people were really listening. It shrank when we were pretending we were interested. Waiting rooms were the worst. In a doctor’s office, the minutes sit in a plastic chair and stare at you. You can feel them gathering behind your eyes, growing heavy.

I began to wonder if time was something the world did to us, or something we did to the world. If the day is an ocean, maybe some people swim and others sink. The clock is there either way, but the experience changes depending on whether you’re moving with it or against it.

It would be comforting to say I became wiser after that. That I learned to savor every second, to become a person who lives fully and gratefully and with intentionality. But if I’m honest, what happened first was not wisdom—it was obsession. I became a collector of sensations, trying to catch time behaving unusually.

I’d stand in line and try to predict when it would “thicken” again. I’d wash dishes and listen for the point where the repetitive motion slipped into something like meditation. I’d scroll through my phone and wonder why the minutes vanished so quickly, as if the screen were draining them into a hidden well.

Sometimes it worked. Sometimes the world would briefly open its hand and show me how many shades of “now” there are.

And then, of course, there were days when nothing happened. I’d go through the same routines, the same traffic patterns, the same polite exchanges with strangers. The clock was always ticking, always obedient. Time behaved. That was the most unsettling part: that the unusual moments were random, not promises. They didn’t arrive on schedule. They were not rewards for mindfulness. They were weather.

On one of those ordinary days, I sat on a bus that was nearly empty. Outside, the city moved in a steady blur. Trees slid by, their leaves flashing in the light like a school of small fish. My reflection appeared faintly in the window: a person superimposed on motion.

At a stop, someone got on and the air changed. I couldn’t explain exactly how. It wasn’t that the temperature shifted. It was more like the bus’s atmosphere recalibrated. The new passenger carried something in them—fatigue, maybe, or relief—and the presence of another human being rearranged my perception.

The bus lurched forward and for a moment time felt normal and ordinary again. I thought: *See? Just me being dramatic.*

Then the next stop came. The doors opened, and the scene outside—the same street corner, the same strip of sky—felt like it belonged to a different timeline. The colors seemed slightly off, not in a hallucination way, but in a way that made me aware of how much our brains correct the world without asking permission. I noticed the spacing between sounds. The world became a diagram for a second: light measured in wavelengths, footsteps measured in pressure, conversation measured in breath.

When the bus doors shut, the sensation dissolved. Time returned to its everyday speed. The moment passed, and yet it left a bruise of awareness behind.

That’s the thing about noticing: it changes the thing you’re noticing. Once you’ve seen the seams, you can’t unsee them.

Eventually, I stopped trying to force time into revelations. I stopped waiting for the “thick” moments like they were signs written in the margins. Instead, I started treating time less like a mystery to solve and more like a companion to learn. I began to ask not, *What is time?* but, *How am I using it?*

There was a shift in my habits. I started keeping small agreements with myself: walk for ten minutes without checking anything; drink water slowly; sit in silence for the duration of a song; answer messages when I meant to answer them, not when I felt obligated. The changes weren’t heroic. They didn’t make headlines or summon a new personality. They were the kind of choices that don’t feel cinematic at the moment you make them.

But after a while, something interesting happened. The ordinary days started to include little places where time could breathe. Not because the universe was suddenly generous, but because I became less frantic. I let the minutes stretch by refusing to yank them shorter.

I also realized that most people aren’t rushing because they’re impatient. They’re rushing because time has become expensive in their minds. We talk about it as if it’s a currency, a limited resource, something you lose if you blink. We measure our lives with appointments and deadlines, and then we wonder why it feels like the days disappear.

There’s a kind of grief in that. Not dramatic grief, not a sobbing kind, but a quiet one that shows up in the background: the sense that life is happening somewhere else, in a future where we’ll finally catch up. We’re always living one task behind, one worry ahead.

I think the first lesson time taught me—though it took me far too long to learn—is that there isn’t a catch-up. There’s only participation. The “future” is not a place where you can wait. It’s where your attention already is, constantly. If you don’t bring your mind with you, it passes through like a visitor who doesn’t leave a footprint.

So I started bringing my mind more often.

Some days it was easy. Other days it wasn’t. Sometimes I still scrolled too much. Sometimes I still snapped at people for reasons I didn’t fully understand until later. Sometimes my thoughts ran like restless animals and time got jagged again. The world didn’t become perfectly kind. I didn’t become a serene monk living beyond the clock.

But I became more forgiving of the fact that time is both structure and flow. A framework you live inside, and also a substance you can’t grip. You can’t hold it, but you can notice it. You can’t stop it, but you can meet it.

Now, when I hear people say they “lost time,” I understand a little differently. Not that time is something you misplace like a phone. It’s more that you can drift out of contact. You can spend hours with your body in one place and your attention in another, then wake up wondering where the day went.

The truth is: the day didn’t go anywhere. The attention did.

And that means something hopeful. It means you can come back. Not to some earlier version of yourself who wasn’t distracted, but to the present moment you’re already in—the one that’s always been waiting in plain sight, humming softly above the everyday noise like a clock you never quite appreciated.

Every now and then, time thickens again. When it does, I don’t try to grab it or demand an explanation. I just let it be what it is: a brief reminder that reality is larger than the way we measure it, and that the most extraordinary thing might simply be the act of paying attention while it happens.
